you know those decisions you keep thinking about for DAYS? 

I do this too.

I'll go back and forth, think of 20 different scenarios, and somehow convince myself I need MORE time to decide.

until I have to tell myself:
'Nats, it's not that serious. You can literally change it later.'

because sometimes I'm giving a decision I can undo tomorrow the same amount of brainpower as something I'll be stuck with for YEARS.

so lately, I've been asking myself
'if I get this wrong, how hard is it to change?'

because not every decision deserves the same amount of thinking.

hiring someone?
signing a long-term contract?
spending a significant amount of money?

of course, those deserve more thought.

but trying a different tool?
testing an idea for a week?
changing a process to see if it works better?

those probably don't need 3 days and 17 imaginary scenarios. 

sometimes you can just try.

see what happens.
keep it if it works.
change it if it doesn't.

so now when I catch myself overthinking, I ask

'Nats.... is this REALLY that serious?' 😂

if I can try it, change it, or completely scrap it later.
I probably don't need another 20 scenarios in my head.

sometimes the decision becomes clearer AFTER you try something, not before. :>

Happy Friday everyone!

Last Friday marked the end of my 6-month contract at Fractile. This Friday marks the end of Week 1 of the job search.

And fair play to everyone currently navigating the 2026 job market… 😅

Times have changed. Looking for a job is no longer just scrolling through LinkedIn and firing off applications. It’s basically a full-scale strategic operation.

A few things I’ve learned/relearned this week:

1️⃣ We desperately need a new rejection template. Surely we can do better than:

“After careful consideration…”

So I’m setting my LinkedIn network a challenge - give me your funniest way to reject a candidate. 😂

2️⃣ Be ready to talk about AI.
I’ve been asked several times how I’ve used AI in TA. If you haven’t used it yet, get curious. Understand where it can genuinely improve recruitment and where human judgement still matters.

3️⃣ Grow a thick skin.
There will be rejection. Lots of it.
People say it’s a numbers game, but I don’t think that means applying for 100 random jobs.

For me, it means being targeted, networking, speaking to people and creating opportunities rather than waiting for them.

4️⃣ Treat the job search like a job.
I’ve genuinely put structure around my days - applications, networking, research, follow-ups and interview prep. However, allow yourself to go for a walk, hit the gym or just have an hour away from the computer. Be kind to yourself. 


And after Week 1?

Still smiling. Still positive. Still looking.

I’ve spent 20 years in Talent Acquisition across agency, RPO/MSP and internal TA, leading teams globally while remaining very hands-on.

My latest contract was in the AI/semiconductor world, and now I’m looking for the next challenge - contract or permanent, and not ego-driven by title.

If you’re hiring, know someone who is, or just fancy a conversation, my inbox is very much open.

And most importantly…
Give me your best rejection line below. 👇

DBS has pledged 600 new hires. Singapore's three biggest banks cut nearly 3,000 roles last year. Both numbers are true. Only one of them is a strategy.

Twice in six weeks, DBS put its hand up.

On 15 July it committed to more than 600 relationship managers, frontline advisors and platform engineers by end-2028, chasing S$1 trillion in wealth and retail assets by 2030.

On 24 August it signed an industry-first skills agreement with the Institute of Banking and Finance Singapore.

Ms Lee Yan Hong, DBS's Head of Group Human Resources, put it on record: "Our philosophy has always been to save people, not jobs."

Read that again. The job goes. The person stays.

Now hold that against the other set of books.

In 2025, DBS shed 1,624 roles.
OCBC shed 333.
UOB shed 849.

Nearly 3,000 people, from the same three banks, are now talking about hiring.

None of them called it a retrenchment exercise. Attrition. Contracts not renewed. Post-merger consolidation. The seats simply stopped being refilled.

I called it a cut in my first line. None of them would.

ManpowerGroup's survey of nearly 600 Singapore employers, fielded in April, put finance and insurance at -2% for this quarter, the weakest of any major industry here, against manufacturing at +25%.

A shrinking sector, hiring hard.

This is the third time I am writing about this. In June it was DBS's then-CEO Mr Piyush Gupta, admitting he was struggling to create jobs. In August it was OCBC's Mr Tan Teck Long, who pledged 600 relationship managers on 1 July and hoped AI would "increase the workforce". Two weeks later DBS named the same number - and calls it saving people, not jobs.

I read that 600 as growth. It is narrower than that.

A pledge tells you which roles are being funded. The headcount tells you which ones quietly stopped being refilled.

They are funding the roles where a human relationship still closes the deal. They are defunding the roles where a process just needs executing.

That same sort is running inside your business right now, named or not.

Here is what I do with a leadership team. Every role goes on the table in two piles: those that survive on relationship and judgement, and those that survive only on process.

The second pile is your next organisation and jobs redesign. Every leader I work with either runs that sort deliberately, or has it run on them later.

💬 Last time you replaced someone, did anyone ask whether the seat should still exist?

4 signs your team is ready for AI. 4 signs it will destroy you if you try. Read both lists before you sign the contract.
The most common question I get from teams considering AI integration: "how do we know if we're ready?" I want to give an honest answer that isn't a vendor pitch.

Signs you ARE ready:

1. The process is documented.
Not perfectly. But there's a written version. Steps have names. Inputs and outputs are describable. New team members can be trained on it in a week or less.

2. You have a baseline you can measure.
Current cycle time, error rate, cost per task, or throughput. Something quantitative. Without a baseline, you can't tell if AI is helping.

3. You have someone accountable for AI outcomes.
Not just "the vendor" or "engineering." A named person who owns whether the AI is behaving as designed and whether the outcomes are improving.

4. Your data is where AI can access it.
Structured. Accessible. Governance-cleared. If your data lives in 14 spreadsheets and one person's inbox, AI is downstream of a data hygiene project you haven't done yet.

Signs you're NOT ready:

1. Nobody agrees on what "good" looks like.
If stakeholders can't articulate what a good output looks like, AI can't hit it. Define first. Then automate.

2. You're automating to avoid a harder conversation.
"Should this process exist?" is the conversation. "Can we AI it?" is the avoidance. Have the first conversation before the second.

3. Your team doesn't have the technical bandwidth.
AI integration is not a "buy the tool and use it" project. It requires evaluation infrastructure, governance, ongoing monitoring, and someone to own model behavior. If you don't have this capacity, budget for it before you start.

4. The stakes are unrecoverable.
For high-stakes decisions — legal filings, medical diagnoses, hiring decisions, immigration cases — the review overhead almost always erases the AI cost advantage. Handle those with humans and use AI to speed the humans' work, not replace it.

The teams doing AI well in 2026 got clear on both lists before they started. Which list is longer for your team right now?

Feeling stuck between endless applications and a flood of “bootcamp” promises is a reality many early‑career professionals face today.  

The underlying issue isn’t a lack of talent; it’s the false belief that a short‑term credential will automatically unlock the next interview. I’ve seen this pattern repeat: fresh graduates pour time and money into intensive programs, only to emerge with another line on their résumé and no clear path to a role. The market rewards proof of ability far more than a badge that looks good on paper.

The antidote is to shift from “credential hunting” to “capability showcasing.” First, identify the core outcomes hiring managers care about-clean data pipelines, actionable visualisations, and the ability to translate insights into business decisions. Then, build a portfolio that mirrors those outcomes. A well‑documented project that cleans a messy dataset, applies a predictive model, and visualises the impact for a mock stakeholder tells a recruiter more than any certificate. Share the process on a personal site or LinkedIn, and tag the tools you used. This creates searchable evidence of competence and invites organic conversation.

Second, leverage targeted networking instead of generic applications. Reach out to alumni from programs you admire, ask for a 15‑minute coffee chat, and focus the conversation on learning about real‑world challenges they face. People are far more willing to help when you demonstrate curiosity about their work than when you simply request a referral. Those interactions often reveal hidden opportunities-internal projects, freelance gigs, or contract work-that bypass the crowded applicant pools entirely.

Finally, treat learning as a continuous loop. Pick one emerging skill, such as generative AI prompting, and apply it immediately to a personal project. The rapid feedback loop reinforces mastery and keeps your profile current without the sunk‑cost pressure of a year‑long bootcamp.

In short, the most reliable shortcut is not a third‑party program but a disciplined habit of building, sharing, and networking around tangible results. When you let your work speak louder than a certificate, the doors start to open on their own.

Join the Mathematics Expert Talent Network | Global Remote 📐🧮
What This Pool Covers,
Pure and applied mathematics; abstract algebra and topology
Real and complex analysis; discrete mathematics and combinatorics
Probability theory and statistics; mathematical modeling and optimization

The research teams behind the best-known AI models come to Mercor for mathematical judgment they can't generate on their own. Instead of posting and pulling listings every time a new initiative kicks off, we maintain a standing mathematics talent pool to draw from on short notice.
💰 Compensation: Most contracts in this field have paid $40 to $75 an hour, set per project by scope and depth.

What the Work Looks Like

Problem Creation: Writing a problem at research or competition level—with statements, intended solutions, and reference answers.

Proof Grading: Evaluating model-written proofs (checking if steps follow logically, edge cases are handled, and theorem hypotheses are satisfied).

Gap Analysis Flagging: Identifying where a model reaches a correct final answer through a flawed argument or convincing sketch that doesn't actually prove it.

What We're Looking For

A graduate degree in mathematics or a related field, or an equivalent research or competition background

Clear written communication (since most work involves explaining your reasoning)

Comfort with ambiguous tasks, and willingness to flag unclear instructions

How It Works

Apply: Submit your resume via the link in Comments and confirm your location.

AI Interview: Take a short, ~20-minute AI interview to verify your background.

Get Matched: When a project needs mathematics expertise, we invite matching people from the pool to that specific listing. It names the rate, the hours, and the client, and any hiring decision is made there.

(Note: This is a standing pool, so this listing does not send out rejections. We reach out whenever a project matches your background, which could be within a week or a few months.)

Most agencies do not struggle to grow because they cannot sell.

They struggle because every new client creates a delivery and cash-flow problem.

You land a web design or SEO contract, then immediately need specialists, software, project management, quality control, and upfront fulfilment cash.

That is why agency infrastructure matters more than simply “outsourcing.”

Here are 4 ways to build a delivery model that can scale:

1. Productise what you sell

Custom scopes create custom delivery problems.

Define clear packages with specific deliverables, timelines, revision limits, responsibilities, and outcomes.

For example, do not sell “SEO services.”

Sell a defined monthly local SEO system: technical monitoring, Google Business Profile optimisation, location pages, content, reporting, and a fixed review process.

Clear scope protects margin and makes fulfilment repeatable.

2. Separate client strategy from production

Your client should experience your agency’s strategy, communication, quality standards, and accountability.

The technical work can be delivered by trusted specialists, contractors, or white-label partners.

But do not outsource your relationship with the client.

Own the brief, the goals, the reporting, the quality check, and the next recommendation. That is where agency value compounds.

3. Match cost structure to revenue timing

Hiring a full-time team before revenue is stable creates fixed costs that keep running even when client work slows down.

A flexible delivery network lets you pay for capacity when work is sold, rather than carrying every specialist on payroll from day one.

The key is not avoiding investment.

It is avoiding fixed overhead before you have repeatable demand and reliable margins.

4. Build systems your client can trust

A white-label dashboard, consistent onboarding, project milestones, approval workflows, reporting templates, and documented processes make a small agency feel organised without pretending to be a large one.

Clients do not pay for the size of your team.

They pay for clarity, progress, results, and confidence that someone is accountable.

The biggest mistake is treating white-label fulfilment as a shortcut.

It is infrastructure.

If your offers, vendor standards, quality control, and client communication are weak, outsourcing will only scale the inconsistency.

But when the system is clear, flexible fulfilment gives you room to grow without turning every new sale into an operational emergency.

If you are building a web design, SEO, or AI automation agency and want to scale delivery without losing control of quality or margins, send me a message. I can help you structure a simple offer, fulfilment workflow, and client experience before you add more overhead.

Room 1. SDET interview, 2021.
The candidate knows Playwright cold. Built three frameworks. Open
source contributor. Answers "how do you structure a page object"
flawlessly.
Then the interviewer asks: "A defect gets past your regression
suite on release day. Walk me through your first hour."
Silence.

Room 2. AI/LLM engineer interview, 2026.
The candidate fine-tuned models. Deployed RAG. Wrote a blog post
on tool calling that hit 200k reads.
Then the interviewer asks: "Your retrieval returns confident wrong
answers under load. Walk me through how you debug the pipeline."
Same silence.

Two different rooms. Same problem: rehearsed knowledge without
rehearsed performance.
I've been on the hiring side for 15 years — Amazon, Visa,
PlayStation, Paytm. Ran 100+ bar-raiser interviews for SDET roles.
The pattern never changed. Candidates who practice daily
outperform candidates who study weekends. Every time.

So I built DailyKnack — a 15-minute daily loop for both rooms.

→ 9 MCQs
→ 1 spoken answer
→ 1 code rep
→ 1 Code Review Drill

Two tracks live today:
• SDET — web automation, API contracts, test data, CI/CD,
  performance, accessibility, contract testing

  memory, evals, multi-agent systems, MCP

Every question is curated from real interviews. Answers are
drafted with AI and reviewed by me — same bar I used as a
bar-raiser.

Anonymous by design. No email, no name. Free tier stays free.
